01 What MXL is

Media shared
in memory

Zero-copy in a host

Media functions on the same host exchange flows via a shared RAM ring buffer. The writer places each frame (grain), making it instantly visible to all readers: zero copies, zero vendor conversion.

Open and vendor-neutral

An Apache-2.0 SDK defining MXL by implementation: memory layouts and timing for v210 video, float32 audio and ST 291 ANC. Delivers the exchange layer specified by the EBU DMF Reference Architecture.

Built for containers

C++ core with C API and Rust bindings. A lightweight, async-by-design library with minimal dependencies, built for on-prem and cloud containers.

3

02 EBU + AMWA

JT-DMF:
four tracks

Synchronisation

End-to-End timing: a unified model for timing and synchronisation across a Dynamic Media Facility (DMF).

Compute resources

Provisioning, scaling and releasing compute, storage, network and media functions. In progress: a vendor-neutral standard for media applications to advertise resource requirements.

Flow connection

How media flows (including MXL) are discovered, described, negotiated and connected across a dynamic facility.

Business activity

The business drivers, commercial models and organisational change needed to adopt dynamic media architectures.

03 Released 9 September 2026

What's new
in MXL v1.1

Headline

mxl-fabrics

Flows cross hosts seamlessly. mxl-fabrics replicates flows between host domains via libfabric. Remote readers use the exact same Flow API as local ones.

Supported transports: RoCEv2 (Verbs) and AWS EFA for accelerated networking; TCP as universal fallback. (Demonstrated live today.)

Tooling

GStreamer plugin

gst-mxl-rs enables reading and writing of MXL flows natively in GStreamer.

Tooling

mxl-data-probe

Tooling to inspect and visualise ancillary data flow content.

API

Multi-flow sync

Synchronise and wait for data across multiple flows, aligned to a single timestamp.

Quality

Fixes and docs

Includes reserved tail grains, thread-safe fabrics, forward-jumping writers and sync-group ordering. Full backward compatibility with the v1.0 API.

  1. mxlCreateInstance(domain, options) Attach to the MXL domain — a directory on tmpfs, typically /dev/shm/mxl.
  2. mxlCreateFlowWriter(instance, flowDef, options, &writer, &configInfo, &created) Create the flow's ring buffer from its NMOS IS-04 definition — or re-open it if it already exists (created says which).
  3. configInfo.common.grainRate · .format · .maxCommitBatchSizeHint Geometry comes back in configInfo. No extra call, and no negotiation with anybody.
  4. mxlGetCurrentIndex(&grainRate) Find where “now” sits on the ST 2059 / TAI timeline. The index comes from the clock, never from a counter.
  5. mxlTimestampToIndex(&editRate, timestampNs) This frame's presentation time becomes the grain index it will occupy.
  6. mxlFlowWriterOpenGrain(writer, index, &grainInfo, &payload) Reserve the slot. The next index, headIndex + 1, lands on the hatched tail grain, which readers are already kept off. payload points straight into shared memory, so you render into the memory the readers will look at.
  7. grainInfo.validSlices = grainInfo.totalSlices; /* dropped frame: grainInfo.flags = MXL_GRAIN_FLAG_INVALID; */ Say how many slices are valid — all of them, or the lines written so far when you commit progressively. A dropped frame is marked on flags instead, and still committed, so the ring advances and readers skip it.
  8. mxlFlowWriterCommitGrain(writer, &grainInfo) Publish. The head moves onto this grain, and readers blocked on the futex wake up. Called once per slice batch when you commit progressively.
  9. mxlSleepForNs(mxlGetNsUntilIndex(nextIndex, &editRate)) Pace to the next grain and loop. Nothing was sent anywhere — the readers are already looking at it.
  10. mxlFlowWriterOpenSamples(writer, sampleIndex, count, &slices) Opens [sampleIndex − count, sampleIndex) in the write half: it must start at or after the head, and count is at most half the buffer. Back come two fragments — the ring wraps — plus the stride between channels.
  11. memcpy(slices.base.fragments[0].pointer + ch * stride, …) Audio is de-interleaved: each channel has its own circular buffer.
  12. mxlFlowWriterCommitSamples(writer) Publish the sample window: the head moves to sampleIndex, and the window joins the read half.
  13. mxlSleepForNs(mxlGetNsUntilIndex(sampleIndex, &sampleRate)) Pace to the next batch and loop.
  14. mxlReleaseFlowWriter(instance, writer); mxlDestroyInstance(instance) Release the writer, then the instance. The flow's files are garbage-collected once its writer lock is gone.
  1. mxlCreateInstance(domain, options) Same domain, a different process. Nothing is shared but the filesystem.
  2. mxlGetFlowDef(instance, flowId, buffer, &bufferSize) Read the flow's NMOS IS-04 definition to configure the pipeline. Call it once with a small buffer to learn the size it needs.
  3. mxlCreateFlowReader(instance, flowId, options, &reader) Map the flow read-only (PROT_READ). No copy, no shared IPC or PID namespace, no handshake with the writer.
  4. mxlFlowReaderGetConfigInfo(reader, &configInfo) Format, grain rate, ring length — the immutable header. mxlFlowReaderGetInfo returns config plus runtime in one shot.
  5. mxlGetTime(); mxlTimestampToIndex(&rate, t) Place the read cursor.
  6. mxlFlowReaderGetGrain(reader, index, timeoutNs, &grainInfo, &payload) Blocks on the futex until that grain is committed. payload is the writer's memory — the grain was never copied.
  7. mxlFlowReaderGetGrainSlice(reader, index, minValidSlices, …) Or wake as soon as N slices are valid, for sub-frame latency. Non-blocking variants exist for both.
  8. if (grainInfo.flags & MXL_GRAIN_FLAG_INVALID) … /* skip */ else if (grainInfo.validSlices == grainInfo.totalSlices) … Skip a dropped frame; process a complete one in place.
  9. mxlFlowReaderGetSamples(reader, index, count, timeoutNs, &slices) Gets [index − count, index). The window must end at or before the head and start no more than half a buffer behind it — the read half; further back is TOO_LATE.
  10. slices.base.fragments[0..1].pointer + ch * stride Two fragments cover the ring wrap; stride hops between de-interleaved channels.
  11. MXL_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE_TOO_EARLY / _TOO_LATE → mxlFlowReaderGetRuntimeInfo(reader, &rt) Ask where the head is and realign the cursor — the normal way a reader recovers from drift.
  12. MXL_ERR_FLOW_INVALID → mxlReleaseFlowReader() + mxlCreateFlowReader() The writer recreated the flow: drop the mapping and re-open it.
  13. mxlIndexToTimestamp(&rate, index); mxlSleepUntil(deadline) Derive the timestamp you hand downstream and pace delivery.
  14. mxlReleaseFlowReader(instance, reader); mxlDestroyInstance(instance) Release the reader, then the instance. The writer never knew you were there.
  1. mxlCreateInstance(domain, options) One instance for the whole function. The reader and the writer below both come from it, because both flows live in the same domain: the process attaches once.
  2. mxlCreateFlowReader(instance, flowIdA, options, &reader) First handle: map flow A read-only. No handshake with A's writer, which never knows this function is there.
  3. mxlCreateFlowWriter(instance, flowDefB, options, &writer, &configInfo, &created) Second handle, same instance: create flow B from its NMOS IS-04 definition. Its format and rate are this function's to choose. They need not match A's.
  4. mxlGetTime(); mxlTimestampToIndex(&rate, t) Place the cursor. The index comes from the TAI clock, never from a counter, so A and B agree on what “now” is without talking.
  5. mxlFlowReaderGetGrain(reader, index, timeoutNs, &inInfo, &in) Wait on the futex for grain index of A, at most its head, the newest committed grain. in is A's writer's memory; nothing was copied.
  6. mxlFlowWriterOpenGrain(writer, index, &outInfo, &out) Open the grain on B. As B's next grain it lands on B's hatched tail slot, which B's readers are kept off until you commit.
  7. process(in, out); outInfo.validSlices = outInfo.totalSlices; Read A in place, render straight into B's shared memory. The processing is the only copy.
  8. mxlFlowWriterCommitGrain(writer, &outInfo) Publish on B: its head moves onto the new grain and B's readers wake. Loop on index + 1.
  9. mxlFlowReaderGetSamples(reader, index, count, timeoutNs, &in) Get [index − count, index) of A from its read half, as two fragments if the window crosses the ring's end.
  10. mxlFlowWriterOpenSamples(writer, index, count, &out) Open the same window on B, in its write half, ahead of B's head.
  11. process(in.base.fragments, out.base.fragments) Channel by channel, ch * stride into each fragment: read A in place, write B in place.
  12. mxlFlowWriterCommitSamples(writer) Publish on B: its head moves to index, and the window joins B's read half. Loop on index + count.
  13. mxlReleaseFlowReader(instance, reader); mxlReleaseFlowWriter(instance, writer) Release both handles, each back to the instance that made it.
  14. mxlDestroyInstance(instance) Once, and last: one instance, torn down after both of its handles.

The MXL domain

where the exchange actually happens

tmpfs volume — RAMno disk
/dev/shm/mxl/the domain
5fbec3b1-….mxl-flow/
data — mxlFlowInfo header
flow_def.json
access
grains/0 … grains/N — the ring
writer — read/write, holds the lock
readers — PROT_READ, any number
  1. mxlIsTmpFs(path, &isTmpFs) A domain is just a directory — but it has to live on tmpfs/ramfs, so every access is a memory access.
  2. ${domain}/${flowId}.mxl-flow/{data, flow_def.json, access} One directory per flow: the mxlFlowInfo header, the NMOS IS-04 definition that describes the media, and the access record.
  3. grains/0 … grains/N ← memory-mapped ring Grains form a ring. The tail entry (hatched) is reserved for the writer, and it comes out of the 200 ms history: readers get one grain less. Continuous flows reserve the tail half of a buffer sized to twice the history, so their readers keep the full 200 ms. Writer and readers never touch the same cell.
  4. mmap(PROT_READ) + futex Readers map read-only and wait on futexes, not POSIX mutexes — so no shared IPC or PID namespace is needed and containers just work. Permissions are plain UNIX, per domain and per flow.
  5. mxlGarbageCollectFlows() The index is derived from wall-clock TAI and the edit rate, so writer and reader never handshake; flows whose writer lock has disappeared are reaped.

Inter-host exchange — MXL Fabrics API

a reader on one host, a writer on the other, RDMA in between

Host Ainitiator
domain — flow in shared memory
libmxl mxlFlowReader + libmxl-fabrics
RDMA remote write · index in immediate data
libfabric · OFI — TCP · VERBS · EFA · SHM
lands in the peer's ring buffer
Host Btarget
libmxl-fabrics + libmxl mxlFlowWriter
domain — the same flow, local again
  1. mxlFabricsCreateInstance(instance, NULL, &fi) A build-time opt-in: the Fabrics API is only compiled with MXL_ENABLE_FABRICS_OFI, which is OFF by default. Same repo, same 1.1 release and same <mxl/…> headers as libmxl — it lands as libmxl-fabrics, linked on top of it.
  2. mxlCreateFlowWriter(…) → mxlFabricsCreateTarget(fi, &target) → mxlFabricsTargetSetup(target, &cfg, options, &targetInfo) The receiving host owns a normal MXL writer, and exposes that ring buffer's memory to the network.
  3. mxlFabricsTargetInfoToString(targetInfo, buf, &size) The address is handed to the other host out of band — the repo ships no signalling protocol; the demo passes a JSON file or a base64 string.
  4. mxlCreateFlowReader(…) → mxlFabricsCreateInitiator(fi, &init) → mxlFabricsInitiatorSetup(init, &cfg, NULL) → mxlFabricsInitiatorAddTarget(init, targetInfo) The sending host is a normal MXL reader — the same API a media function uses. Nothing about the flow changes because it is going off-box.
  5. mxlFlowReaderGetGrainSlice(…) → mxlFabricsInitiatorTransferGrain(init, grainIndex, startSlice, validSlices) Read a slice locally, then RDMA-write it straight into the peer's ring buffer. Grain index and slice range travel in the RDMA immediate data.
  6. mxlFabricsTargetReadGrain(target, timeoutMs, &grainIndex) → mxlFlowWriterOpenGrain(…) → mxlFlowWriterCommitGrain(…) On the far side there is nothing to copy: the payload already landed by DMA, so the target only opens and commits the grain — and local readers wake as usual.
  7. mxlFabricsInitiatorMakeProgressBlocking(init, 250) Providers today: TCP, VERBS, EFA and SHM, remote-write only. This is the one place a copy crosses a boundary — and it is the IT industry's transport, not ours.

Glossary

the words on this slide

Domain

A directory holding a set of flows on a host — /dev/shm/mxl by default. It must sit on tmpfs, and several domains can coexist on one host.

Flow

One piece of media: a video essence, an audio essence, an ANC stream. An NMOS IS-04 term. On disk it is a ring buffer, not a stream.

flow-id

The flow's UUID, and the only name a reader needs. It names the directory <flow-id>.mxl-flow/ and the ?id= in an MXL URI.

flow-def

flow_def.json in the flow's directory — its NMOS IS-04 Flow resource: format, grain rate, geometry. The writer writes it, readers read it: the whole handshake.

Grain

One time-addressed unit of a discrete flow: a video frame, or a set of ANC packets. Also IS-04. One ring entry, one file grains/<n>.

Samples

Samples is a number of audio sample for all channels in the flow, defined by the param count in mxlFlowWriterOpenSamples.

Index

A position on the ST 2059-1 timeline, not in a queue: index = timestamp ÷ edit-rate period. Both sides derive it from the clock, so they never handshake.

Slice

The smallest thing committable to a grain — for video, one line of the picture. validSlices of totalSlices lets a reader wake on part of a frame.

Fragment

Not a media concept: when a sample window straddles the ring's wrap point it comes back as two byte ranges, fragments[2].

NMOS IS-04

The AMWA registration and discovery spec. MXL adopts its Flow and Grain definitions wholesale, and flow_def.json is an IS-04 Flow resource.

SMPTE ST 2059-1

Defines the broadcast epoch and clock. Index 0 is that epoch. MXL leverages the definition only — it needs no PTP or ST 2059 time source.

tmpfs

A filesystem that lives in RAM, never on disk. A domain has to be on one — mxlIsTmpFs() checks — so every file access is a memory access.

mmap

Maps a file into a process's address space. Readers map PROT_READ, so a flow can live on a read-only volume. This is what makes the exchange zero-copy.

futex

Linux fast userspace mutex — how readers are woken. A POSIX mutex would need write access in shared memory; a futex does not, so readers stay read-only.

TAI

International Atomic Time — no leap seconds, so it only ever moves forward. Every MXL index is derived from TAI against the ST 2059-1 epoch.

RDMA

Remote Direct Memory Access: the NIC writes into the peer host's memory without waking its CPU. MXL Fabrics uses remote-write only.

libfabric

The OpenFabrics Interfaces (OFI) user-space API. One API over several transports, so MXL Fabrics never codes to a particular NIC.

VERBS

User-space and kernel-space software interface used ot interact directly with RDMA-capable NICs (e.g.ConnectX).

RoCE v2

RDMA over Converged Ethernet v2 — RDMA carried in UDP on ordinary routable Ethernet, so no InfiniBand fabric is needed. Reached via the verbs provider.

EFA

AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter — Amazon's RDMA transport, libfabric's efa provider, connectionless RDM endpoints. This is the cloud path.

SHM

libfabric's shm provider — same-host transfer through shared memory. Note: libfabric's shared memory, not MXL's. Local flows never need it.

04 The measurement

What the number means

Every grain carries the writer's mxlGetTime() timestamp in its initial bytes. Upon arrival, the reader calculates transit time by comparing this against its local clock.

  • Same host: both ends share a single clock, measuring pure shared-memory propagation.
  • Cross-host: spans two host clocks, synchronised via NTP to a Meinberg grandmaster within tens of microseconds.
  • Testbed: two Dell R760xs servers (2× Xeon Silver 4510, 256 GB RAM, 1× NVIDIA ConnectX-7 at 200 GbE). TCP and Verbs share the same NIC, so only the transport layer varies.

06 Takeaways

What to
take home

In a host, it's free

On a single host, MXL transfers grains via zero-copy shared memory. Inter-process latency is practically zero.

Across hosts, pick the fabric

TCP offers universal compatibility. Switching to RDMA (Verbs) on the same NIC reduces transit latency by 4.7×, making transport choice key to your latency budget.

Same API either way

Remote readers use the exact same Flow API as local ones. mxl-fabrics handles cross-host replication without altering media application code.
